title: A Survey into the Lives of the Infallible Imams

concepts.title: Ch3 — Zayn al-'Abidin as champion of spirituality
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari presents Imam Zayn al-'Abidin ('Ali ibn al-Husayn) as a model of authentic Islamic spirituality, using the Prophet's Household as an example of belief becoming deeply embodied. His worship is described as a genuine journey of the soul toward Allah rather than merely an outward bodily act.

concepts.title: Ch3 — Absorption in worship
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari illustrates the Imam's intense devotion through the incident of his child suffering a broken bone while the Imam was absorbed in worship. The family treated the child without interrupting him, and the next morning he noticed the bandage and asked what had happened. The story is used to convey the depth of his spiritual concentration.

concepts.title: Ch3 — The herald of affection
concepts.explanation: Zayn al-'Abidin is described as a herald of affection who deliberately showed kindness to isolated people, strangers, the poor and those overlooked by society. He invited people such as lepers into his home and cared for them. Mutahhari characterizes his home as a place for the poor, orphans and helpless.

concepts.title: Ch3 — Service in the Hajj caravan
concepts.explanation: During Hajj, Zayn al-'Abidin preferred to travel with a caravan whose members did not know his identity, so that he could serve them without being treated as a distinguished descendant of the Prophet. When they discovered who he was, they wanted to reverse the roles, but he explained that he had deliberately chosen an unfamiliar caravan to gain the opportunity to serve Muslims and friends.

concepts.title: Ch3 — Serving Islam through another form of mission
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari contrasts Zayn al-'Abidin's circumstances with the opportunities given to Imam al-Husayn and Imam al-Sadiq. Although he did not rise with the sword, Mutahhari argues that service to Islam can take different forms and highlights the Imam's legacy through prayer and supplication as one such form.

concepts.title: Ch3 — Mourning Imam al-Husayn as preservation of Karbala's message
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari rejects the interpretation that Zayn al-'Abidin's continual mourning meant merely uncontrolled grief or that he allowed Karbala to be forgotten. He interprets the mourning as a way of preserving the memory of Imam al-Husayn's tragedy and reminding people of why he rose and who was responsible for his death. The Imam's comparison with Ya'qub's grief for Yusuf is used to explain the depth of his sorrow after witnessing the deaths of members of his family.

concepts.title: Ch4 — Why Imam al-Sadiq declined the political opening
concepts.explanation: The end of Umayyad rule created a major political opening because opposition had accumulated among Arabs and Persians through religious discontent, oppression, and the memory of Alawid uprisings. Mutahhari's central question is why Imam al-Sadiq did not seize this opportunity.

concepts.title: Ch4 — Abbasid secret organization and the use of Islamic slogans
concepts.explanation: The Abbasids exploited anti-Umayyad discontent through a secret, organized missionary network, especially in Khorasan. Their public slogans invoked the Household of the Prophet and Qur'anic ideas rather than an explicit Abbasid succession claim, allowing them to mobilize broad support.

concepts.title: Ch4 — Abu Muslim and Abu Salmah
concepts.explanation: The Abbasid movement relied especially on Abu Muslim in Khorasan and Abu Salmah Khallal in Kufah. Mutahhari distinguishes political effectiveness from moral character and describes the two as important operators within the movement.

concepts.title: Ch4 — Abu Salmah's double letter
concepts.explanation: Near the transition to Abbasid rule, Abu Salmah secretly sent essentially the same offer to Imam al-Sadiq and 'Abd Allah al-Mahd, offering to redirect the caliphate toward the family of Abu Talib. The parallel letters reveal the political nature of the proposal.

concepts.title: Ch4 — Imam al-Sadiq burns Abu Salmah's letter
concepts.explanation: Imam al-Sadiq did not even read Abu Salmah's letter; he burned it and sent back a poem illustrating the danger of someone doing the work while another person reaps its outcome. Mutahhari interprets this as evidence that Abu Salmah was not acting as the Imam's sincere follower.

concepts.title: Ch4 — Imam al-Sadiq and 'Abd Allah al-Mahd
concepts.explanation: 'Abd Allah al-Mahd was enthusiastic about Abu Salmah's offer. Imam al-Sadiq challenged the claim that Khorasanis were his followers and warned that the proposed political venture lacked the necessary real conditions.

concepts.title: Ch4 — The Abwa' gathering and Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah
concepts.explanation: Before the Abbasid victory, leaders of Banu Hashim gathered at Abwa'. Muhammad, son of 'Abd Allah al-Mahd, was presented as a potential leader against the Umayyads and was associated by some with the promised Mahdi because of his name and other coincidental features.

concepts.title: Ch4 — Mahdism versus enjoining good and forbidding evil
concepts.explanation: When asked to pledge allegiance to Muhammad as the promised Mahdi, Imam al-Sadiq refused the Mahdi claim but stated that he would pledge support if the movement were genuinely undertaken under the principle of enjoining good and forbidding evil and fighting oppression. This distinction is central to his political stance.

concepts.title: Ch4 — Imam al-Sadiq's foresight concerning the Abbasids
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari presents Imam al-Sadiq as recognizing that the Abbasid political actors had their own ambitions and that Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah would be killed rather than become caliph. The later historical outcome is presented as confirmation within the narrative.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Martyrdom as a shared pattern among the Imams
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari opens by stressing that, in his account, the infallible Imams other than the living Imam of the Time all died as martyrs. He argues that their methods should not be contrasted as though Imam al-Husayn alone resisted oppression while the others accepted it: the objective was resistance to oppressive rule, while the form of combat changed according to circumstances. It could be open warfare, condemnation and social resistance, or covert action under taqiyyah.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Imam Musa al-Kazim's imprisonment and refusal to submit
concepts.explanation: According to the text's account, Imam Musa al-Kazim spent about four years imprisoned and was moved among several prisons. Offers were repeatedly made that he could gain freedom by apologizing, confessing wrongdoing, or otherwise submitting to Harun. He refused these proposals. Mutahhari presents this refusal as an expression of the Imam's resistance and fidelity to his principles.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Basrah prison: 'Isa ibn Ja'far's change of view
concepts.explanation: The Imam was first held in Basrah under 'Isa ibn Ja'far. Although 'Isa initially accepted the government's portrayal of Musa al-Kazim as a political threat, personal contact changed his view: he came to see the Imam as a spiritual man and treated him well. When Harun secretly ordered him to get rid of the Imam, 'Isa refused and asked that the Imam be transferred rather than killed.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Baghdad prisons and the failure of Harun's pressure
concepts.explanation: In Baghdad the Imam was successively placed with Fadl ibn Rabi' and Fadl ibn Yahya al-Barmaki. Each, according to the narrative, became impressed by him and improved his conditions, effectively treating him more like an honored guest than a prisoner. Harun responded by transferring the Imam again and punishing or disfavoring those who treated him sympathetically, eventually placing him with Sindi ibn Shahik, where the conditions became harsh.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Harun's demand for a confession and the Imam's final refusal
concepts.explanation: Near the end of the imprisonment, Harun sent an intermediary with a private offer: if the Imam would simply confess wrongdoing and ask the caliph's forgiveness, he would be released. The text presents this as a test of whether the Imam would legitimize the ruler by an act of submission. Musa al-Kazim refused, indicating that his life was already nearing its end. The narrative then states that he was poisoned about a week later.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Why Harun regarded Imam al-Kazim as a threat
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that Harun's fear was not based on an overt military uprising by the Imam. Rather, Harun perceived the Imam's spiritual authority and popularity as a rival source of legitimacy, especially while arranging allegiance to his sons as future rulers. The Imam's lineage, piety and influence could draw people's attention away from the caliphate. The text therefore describes a 'spiritual revolution' as the deeper threat perceived by Harun.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Ma'mun's account of Harun's respect and political fear
concepts.explanation: The chapter recounts a report attributed to Ma'mun in which Harun showed striking respect toward Musa ibn Ja'far during Hajj, welcomed him while remaining seated on horseback, asked about his family and financial circumstances, and arranged for him to be escorted out. In the account, Harun later explains that the Ahl al-Bayt were political rivals: if their material resources became strong, their supporters could potentially rally around them. Mutahhari uses this story to illustrate the tension between Harun's personal recognition of the Imam's stature and his political fear of that influence.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Spiritual influence as a form of propagation
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari emphasizes that the Imam's influence did not depend on armies or formal propaganda. People who encountered his worship, generosity and character could be transformed by that example. The chapter illustrates this with reports involving 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, an undercover Shi'ah official in Harun's government, and an Ahwazi believer whose heavy tax burden was resolved after the Imam sent a private letter to the governor. The broader lesson in the text is that action and character can propagate religious truth more powerfully than words alone.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Worship and care for the vulnerable as recurring Imam traditions
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari identifies two recurring characteristics among the Imams: profound worship, fear of Allah and monotheistic consciousness; and personal sympathy with the weak, oppressed, dispossessed and needy. He presents these not as abstract ideals but as habits repeatedly visible in the lives of the Imams. For Musa al-Kazim, the chapter connects intense worship with the prison setting and connects religious leadership with direct concern for believers in difficulty.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Bishr Hafi: the Imam's indirect reform through a single question
concepts.explanation: The story of Bishr Hafi illustrates the Imam's ability to reform without coercion. Passing a house where music, dancing and gambling were taking place, Musa al-Kazim asked a servant whether the house belonged to a free man or a slave. The Imam's point was that someone enslaved to Allah would not behave in such a way. Bishr understood the message, sought the Imam, and declared that from that moment he wanted to become Allah's servant. Mutahhari uses the episode as another example of spiritual influence through character and concise guidance.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Safwan Jammal and complicity with an oppressor
concepts.explanation: Safwan Jammal, a companion of the Imam who rented camels, had contracted to provide transportation for Harun's pilgrimage. Musa al-Kazim challenged him about whether he inwardly wished Harun to remain alive long enough to complete the journey and pay the remaining rent. When Safwan admitted that he did, the Imam taught that being content with an oppressor's survival for one's own material interest was itself morally problematic. Safwan then sold his camels and ended that business relationship. Harun discovered the reason and treated the Imam's influence as a serious threat.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Harun's attempts to break the Imam's resistance
concepts.explanation: The chapter gives several examples of attempts to soften or compromise the Imam: promises of release, better accommodation, special food and private assurances that the caliph did not personally regard him as sinful. The Imam repeatedly refused to become dependent on Harun or to validate his authority through apology. One episode has the Imam repeatedly beginning another prayer rather than giving Fadl ibn Rabi' an opportunity to deliver Harun's message, illustrating deliberate refusal to engage with the proposed terms.

concepts.title: Ch5 — The reported method of Imam al-Kazim's martyrdom
concepts.explanation: The final section reports that the Imam was held by Sindi ibn Shahik and that a poisoned preparation was administered to him. According to the narrative, officials then assembled respected people and attempted to demonstrate publicly that he was healthy and had not been harmed. The Imam contradicted this claim, saying that he had been poisoned and had only a short time left. After his death, the authorities reportedly displayed his body by the Baghdad bridge for several days and claimed that he had died naturally.

concepts.title: Ch5 — Mutahhari's three-part explanation of the martyrdom
concepts.explanation: At the conclusion, Mutahhari summarizes three factors behind the martyrdom: first, the Imam's very presence and spiritual authority threatened the ruling caliphs; second, the Imams opposed and exposed oppression while practicing taqiyyah so that they did not unnecessarily leave evidence that could be exploited against them; and third, the Imams possessed an exceptional spirit of resistance and could not be induced to surrender or become obedient followers of the ruler. The chapter's central logic is therefore: different historical forms of resistance do not imply acceptance of oppression.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — The historical problem of al-Rida as crown prince
concepts.explanation: The chapter examines why Imam al-Rida accepted the position of successor under Ma'mun even though the Abbasids had a long record of conflict with the Alawis. Mutahhari frames this as a historical problem comparable to Imam al-Hassan's peace: in both cases critics can argue that accepting an arrangement with an existing caliph amounted to compromise, while the Imam's defenders must explain the circumstances.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Abbasid hostility toward the Alawis
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari describes sustained Abbasid persecution of the Alawis, including imprisonment and killing under Mansur and later rulers. He uses the treatment of their own rivals and even members of the Abbasid dynasty to establish that political power in this period was marked by severe internal rivalry as well as conflict with the Alawis.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — The historical sources for the succession episode
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari says the account should not be reconstructed solely from Shi'ah sources. He compares reports in Shaykh Mufid's al-Irshad and Shaykh Saduq's 'Uyun al-Akhbar al-Rida with Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani's Maqatil al-Talibiyyin, which he identifies as a non-Shi'ah historical source. He argues that important details in these traditions substantially correspond.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Was Ma'mun sincere? Competing historical possibilities
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari lays out several hypotheses rather than claiming certainty: Ma'mun may initially have sincerely intended to transfer authority; Fadl ibn Sahl may have initiated the policy; or Ma'mun may have adopted the proposal for political purposes from the beginning. The chapter explicitly says historical evidence does not establish one explanation with absolute certainty.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Ma'mun's reported Shi'ah sympathies versus political conduct
concepts.explanation: The chapter presents reports of Ma'mun's intellectual interest in Shi'ism and his respect for the Ahl al-Bayt, alongside his father's harsh treatment of Imam Musa al-Kazim and Ma'mun's own political behavior. Mutahhari uses this tension to caution against treating intellectual sympathy or personal admiration as equivalent to political loyalty.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — The oath Ma'mun said he made during his struggle with Amin
concepts.explanation: One historical explanation accepted by Shaykh Saduq and others is that Ma'mun, fearing defeat by his brother Amin, performed purification, prayer and Qur'anic recitation and vowed that if Allah gave him victory he would return the caliphate to its rightful owners. After his victories, he presented the appointment of Imam al-Rida as fulfillment of that oath. Mutahhari presents this as one probability, not as settled fact.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Fadl ibn Sahl as an alternative initiator
concepts.explanation: Another hypothesis is that Fadl ibn Sahl, Ma'mun's powerful minister, proposed bringing Imam al-Rida into the succession. Mutahhari questions explanations that portray Fadl simply as a sincere Shi'ah supporter, noting reports that Imam al-Rida himself distrusted Fadl and warned Ma'mun about him. The chapter leaves Fadl's exact motivation unresolved.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Political theory: attracting Iranian support
concepts.explanation: One proposed political explanation is that Ma'mun wanted to attract Iranian support by associating his government with the Alawis. Mutahhari notes the symbolic importance of the title 'al-Rida' and suggests that presenting the Imam as successor could make it appear that long-standing Iranian sympathy for the family of the Prophet had finally been accommodated.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Political theory: neutralizing Alawi rebellions
concepts.explanation: A second political explanation is that placing Imam al-Rida inside the government could weaken recurring Alawi uprisings. If the most prominent Alawi were publicly incorporated into the succession, other rebels could lose a powerful argument that the Alawis were excluded from government. Mutahhari presents this as a hypothesis about Ma'mun's political calculation.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Political theory: disarming Imam al-Rida's opposition
concepts.explanation: A third proposed motive is to neutralize the Imam himself by giving him a government position. Critics could then say that the Alawi claim to justice changed once its representatives received office. Mutahhari describes the general political principle as giving an opponent a position so that his opposition becomes harder to mobilize.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — The journey from Medina to Marw
concepts.explanation: The chapter identifies the forced summons of Imam al-Rida from Medina to Marw as a significant historical fact. He was brought with relatives under surveillance, and the route was deliberately selected through Basrah and Khuzistan toward Nishapur rather than through Kufah, where he might encounter Shi'ah supporters. Mutahhari emphasizes that the journey was organized without prior consultation with the Imam.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — The Imam's initial refusal
concepts.explanation: According to the historical reports discussed, Imam al-Rida rejected the proposal when it was presented in Marw. Fadl ibn Sahl and al-Hasan ibn Sahl reportedly warned that refusal meant execution; even after the threat was made explicit, the Imam continued to refuse until Ma'mun personally threatened his life.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Acceptance under threat
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari interprets the eventual acceptance as compelled by a threat to the Imam's life. He compares Ma'mun's argument invoking Imam 'Ali's participation in the earlier council with the historical question of whether the Imam was voluntarily accepting the office or submitting to circumstances. This is presented as an important distinction for understanding the event.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — Imam al-Rida's condition of non-interference
concepts.explanation: The Imam agreed on the explicit condition that he would not interfere in government affairs or assume responsibility for Ma'mun's actions. This preserved a distinction between accepting the title and cooperating with the government. Mutahhari notes that the Imam continued to maintain distance from governmental responsibilities, including initially declining to lead the 'Id prayer.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — The 'Id prayer episode
concepts.explanation: When Ma'mun later insisted that Imam al-Rida lead the 'Id prayer, the Imam initially objected that this violated the condition of non-involvement. He eventually agreed but proceeded in a manner that, according to the narrative, generated such popular excitement that Ma'mun and Fadl feared a political upheaval and stopped him before he reached the destination.

concepts.title: Ch6 S1 — The acceptance ceremony and the Imam's independent stance
concepts.explanation: At the formal acceptance ceremony, Imam al-Rida delivered a short speech that did not flatter or thank Ma'mun in the conventional manner. Mutahhari interprets the speech as a concise declaration that accepting the position did not mean accepting Ma'mun's political legitimacy or becoming his collaborator.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — What is certain and what is doubtful
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari separates the succession episode into definite historical facts and doubtful interpretations. He treats the forced summons to Marw, the initial refusal, the threat of death, the eventual acceptance, and the condition of non-interference as firm elements; the precise motives behind Ma'mun's policy remain matters for historical analysis.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — The succession was initiated by Ma'mun, not Imam al-Rida
concepts.explanation: The chapter states that the crown-prince arrangement was not initiated by Imam al-Rida. Ma'mun's agents gathered people from Khorasan and summoned Banu Hashim from Medina before discussing the proposal with the Imam. The route was deliberately chosen to minimize contact with Shi'ah communities.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Imam al-Rida's logical refusal of the caliphate offer
concepts.explanation: When Ma'mun reportedly proposed transferring the caliphate, Imam al-Rida answered that Ma'mun could not legitimately give away something that was either rightfully his or not rightfully his. If it was divinely legitimate, Ma'mun had no right to surrender it; if it was illegitimate, he had no right to transfer it. Mutahhari uses this reasoning to show why the Imam rejected the offer.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Ma'mun combines argument with threat
concepts.explanation: After the Imam rejected the proposal, Ma'mun invoked Imam 'Ali's participation in the six-person council established by 'Umar and used that precedent as a justification for demanding compliance. The argument was accompanied by an explicit threat to kill Imam al-Rida. Mutahhari therefore distinguishes the rational argument Ma'mun offered from the coercive force behind the decision.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — The non-interference condition
concepts.explanation: Imam al-Rida accepted the crown-prince title only with the condition that he would have no practical role in government: no judgments, appointments, dismissals, administration, or other governmental duties. Mutahhari treats this condition as evidence that the Imam did not regard the appointment as ordinary political collaboration.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — The crown-prince speech
concepts.explanation: At the formal ceremony, Ma'mun arranged an elaborate public event, but Imam al-Rida's speech was extremely brief and did not praise or thank Ma'mun. Its substance, as Mutahhari interprets it, was that the Ahl al-Bayt possessed the underlying right to the caliphate and that accepting the title did not mean receiving that right from Ma'mun.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — The 'Id prayer demonstrates the separation
concepts.explanation: When Ma'mun later asked Imam al-Rida to lead the 'Id prayer, the Imam reminded him of their agreement. When he finally agreed on the condition that he would follow his grandfather's manner rather than contemporary court custom, the public response became so intense that Ma'mun ordered him brought back. Mutahhari uses this as evidence of the Imam's independent religious authority.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — The Fadl ibn Sahl hypothesis
concepts.explanation: One disputed explanation is that Fadl ibn Sahl, Ma'mun's powerful minister, initiated the crown-prince arrangement. Some historians have attributed sincere Shi'ah motives to Fadl, but Mutahhari argues that this interpretation conflicts with Imam al-Rida's own distrust of Fadl and his refusal to cooperate with him.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — The alternative Fadl hypothesis
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari considers another hypothesis: if Fadl initiated the policy, his goal may have been to use the Alawi Imam for a larger political project involving Iranian interests. He stresses that this is an assumption, not an established historical fact, and examines it as one possible explanation for the Imam's refusal to cooperate with Fadl.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Baghdad's reaction to the appointment
concepts.explanation: When news of Imam al-Rida's appointment reached Baghdad, Abbasid leaders rejected Ma'mun's decision and pledged allegiance to another Abbasid, Ibrahim ibn Shiklah. Mutahhari uses this reaction to argue that even a successful transfer of power in Khorasan would not automatically have produced unified control over the wider Islamic territories.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Ma'mun's motives remain disputed
concepts.explanation: If Ma'mun initiated the appointment, Mutahhari considers two broad possibilities: he may initially have had a genuine intention to transfer authority, later changing his mind; or the entire arrangement may have been a political maneuver. He reports Shaykh Saduq's account of an oath Ma'mun made during his conflict with Amin while noting that many scholars reject the idea of sincere intentions from the beginning.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Possible political purpose: discrediting Imam al-Rida
concepts.explanation: One political interpretation is that Ma'mun wanted to draw Imam al-Rida into the governmental system so that public dissatisfaction with the government would also damage the Imam's reputation. Mutahhari describes the general political tactic as giving a respected critic an official position and then making the position fail or become unpopular.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Imam al-Rida's opposition to Fadl ibn Sahl
concepts.explanation: The chapter reports traditions in which Fadl ibn Sahl and Hisham ibn Ibrahim approached Imam al-Rida and proposed killing Ma'mun so that the Imam could become caliph. The Imam rejected the proposal and later warned Ma'mun about them. Mutahhari presents this as evidence that the Imam did not regard Fadl's political maneuvering as trustworthy.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Why acceptance could still be religiously justified
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari asks whether Imam al-Rida should simply have accepted death rather than the crown-prince title. He distinguishes this from Imam al-Husayn's situation: al-Husayn faced an explicit demand for allegiance to Yazid and a historical need for public awakening, whereas al-Rida faced a different choice in which accepting a formal position under coercion did not necessarily constitute the same kind of religious compromise.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Cooperation with rulers: Safwan Jammal and 'Ali ibn Yaqtin
concepts.explanation: The chapter compares two apparently opposite examples. Imam Musa al-Kazim condemned Safwan Jammal's cooperation with Harun when it served Safwan's personal financial interest and included wishing for Harun's survival. By contrast, he encouraged 'Ali ibn Yaqtin to remain inside the Abbasid system while concealing his Shi'ism because his position could serve believers. Mutahhari's distinction is between being used by the ruling system and using a position to serve religious and social purposes.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — The example of Prophet Yusuf
concepts.explanation: Imam al-Rida is reported to have defended his position by comparing it with Prophet Yusuf's acceptance of administrative authority under the Egyptian ruler. Yusuf sought responsibility over the storehouses in order to use the position for a beneficial purpose; Imam al-Rida contrasted that voluntary request with his own forced acceptance. The example supports the principle that cooperation is evaluated partly by purpose and circumstances.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — Wilayat al-ja'ir and conditional cooperation
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari connects the discussion to the jurisprudential concept of undertaking a position under an unjust ruler. Although such cooperation is ordinarily prohibited, he explains that it can become permissible, recommended, or obligatory when the position is genuinely necessary to enjoin good, prevent evil, reduce oppression, or serve the Muslim community. The determining issue is the purpose and effect of the cooperation.

concepts.title: Ch6 S2 — The practical result of Imam al-Rida's appointment
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that the crown-prince episode did not accomplish Ma'mun's presumed purpose of making Imam al-Rida a normal participant in government. Instead, the Imam retained his independence, his qualifications became more publicly visible, and the Ahl al-Bayt's standing was strengthened. The chapter therefore uses the episode to illustrate how the same outward act—holding a government position—can have different meanings depending on who controls its purpose.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Imam al-'Askari under extreme pressure
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari presents Imam al-Hassan al-'Askari as an Imam who lived under unusually severe surveillance. His residence in Samarra was imposed by the authorities and located in the military quarter, allowing close monitoring.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Samarra and the military quarter
concepts.explanation: The government center had been transferred to Samarra, and Imam al-Hadi and Imam al-'Askari were compelled to reside in the area called al-'Askar/al-'Askari, associated with the army. The location itself functioned as a mechanism of surveillance.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Six years of Imamate
concepts.explanation: Imam al-'Askari's Imamate lasted six years. Mutahhari states that during this period he was either imprisoned or, when free, prevented from normal social contact and visits.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Dignity as a defining quality
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari highlights dignity and impressive bearing as especially characteristic of Imam al-'Askari. Reports describe even opponents and officials being affected by his presence and showing respect toward him.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Why surveillance intensified
concepts.explanation: According to the chapter, people knew that the awaited Imam al-Mahdi was expected to emerge from Imam al-'Askari's lineage. Mutahhari compares the authorities' surveillance with Pharaoh's attempt to prevent the birth foretold among Bani Isra'il.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Searches for the promised child
concepts.explanation: Authorities repeatedly searched the Imam's house, particularly around his death, because they had heard reports that his son, the future Imam al-Mahdi, had already been born.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Concealed birth of Imam al-Mahdi
concepts.explanation: The chapter describes the birth as concealed from the general public, with only a limited group aware of it. Imam al-Mahdi was about six years old when his father died, according to the account presented.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Searches of the women in the household
concepts.explanation: After Imam al-'Askari's death, officials searched the household and examined women to identify a possible pregnancy. One slave girl was detained for a year because officials suspected she was pregnant, but the suspicion proved mistaken.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Lady Hudayth and the title Jaddah
concepts.explanation: The mother of Imam al-'Askari is identified as Hudayth and was known as Jaddah, 'grandmother,' because of her relationship to the Imam of the Time. Mutahhari emphasizes that her reputation rested on her own status and learning, not merely her family relationship.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Jaddah as a Shi'ah refuge
concepts.explanation: After Imam al-'Askari's death, Jaddah is described as a learned refuge for Shi'ahs. People brought religious and doctrinal questions to her.

concepts.title: Ch7 — Hakimah Khatun and the hidden Imam
concepts.explanation: Hakimah Khatun explained that Imam al-'Askari's hidden son was the true Imam during occultation, while people should refer to Jaddah for practical questions. She compared this arrangement with Imam al-Husayn leaving much of his outward trust to Zaynab while the true successor was Imam Zayn al-'Abidin.

concepts.title: Ch7 — The central paradox of the chapter
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari's central lesson is that extraordinary political surveillance could not prevent the succession that Shi'ah belief understood as divinely ordained. The authorities attempted to control the circumstances surrounding the birth and succession, while the Imam's spiritual authority continued through concealment and trusted intermediaries.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Two essential prophetic missions
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari presents two central purposes for the prophets: establishing the correct relationship between human beings and God through tawhid, and establishing just relations among people through justice, peace, cooperation, benevolence, affection and service.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Justice as the general prophetic mission
concepts.explanation: Using Qur'anic language about the Book, Balance and establishing justice, Mutahhari argues that justice among humanity is a general aim of prophetic missions.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Universal justice defined
concepts.explanation: Universal justice means a future in which tyranny, oppression, discrimination, war, hatred, bloodshed, exploitation and their associated deception no longer dominate human society.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Justice is not merely an afterlife promise
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari contrasts the idea that justice belongs only to the next world with the Islamic expectation of a future transformation of earthly human society.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Three questions about justice
concepts.explanation: The discussion is organized around three questions: What is justice? Is the inclination toward justice present in human nature? And is justice practically achievable, and by what means?

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Definition of justice
concepts.explanation: Justice is presented as giving each person what they are entitled to on the basis of their creation, qualifications and activities; it is contrasted with oppression and discrimination.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Justice versus discrimination
concepts.explanation: Justice does not mean mechanically giving everyone identical treatment. Mutahhari distinguishes equal status from cases where differing eligibility or merit can justify differing outcomes.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Is justice instinctive?
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari asks whether humans can value justice for its own sake, even where personal benefit is absent, just as humans naturally appreciate beauty and seek knowledge.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Nietzsche and Machiavelli's position as presented
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari describes one philosophical position as treating power as fundamental and justice as a concept produced by the weak. He associates this position with Nietzsche and Machiavelli.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Bertrand Russell's position as presented
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari describes another position as accepting justice because enlightened self-interest eventually shows that individual interests depend on justice for all.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Critique of self-interest alone
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that a justice system based only on calculated self-interest becomes vulnerable when an individual or group acquires enough power to act without fear of retaliation.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Marxist theory as presented
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari describes a third approach in which economic and productive conditions are expected to produce justice automatically through historical development toward socialism.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — The Islamic view of human nature
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari presents the Islamic position as rejecting pessimism about human nature: people can be educated and spiritually developed until justice becomes genuinely desired, even against personal interest.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — 'Ali ibn Abi Talib as an example
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari invokes Imam 'Ali as an example of a person whose commitment to justice was not reducible to personal advantage, arguing that such examples demonstrate the possibility of justice-oriented human beings.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Mahdism as human perfection
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that the reappearance of the Imam of the Time should not be understood as humanity returning to primitive conditions. He describes it as an intellectual, moral and scientific elevation of humanity.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — The question of the Imam's long life
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari addresses doubts about the Imam's long lifespan by arguing that current scientific knowledge does not establish the complete limits of natural possibility and that major transitions in the history of life are not fully explained.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Characteristics of the Mahdi's age
concepts.explanation: The promised age is described through traditions as an age of justice, security, spiritual wealth, reduced poverty and hatred, fair distribution, and renewed vitality of Qur'an and Sunnah.

concepts.title: Ch8 P1 — Al-Qa'im and the meaning of rising
concepts.explanation: The title al-Qa'im is connected to the one who rises. Mutahhari links the title with the establishment of justice and the restoration of religious guidance.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Mahdism predates the third century AH
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari's historical argument begins by rejecting the idea that belief in Mahdism originated only around the birth of Imam al-Mahdi in the middle of the third century AH.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Qur'anic foundations
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari points to Qur'anic promises concerning the inheritance of the earth by righteous servants and the eventual triumph of true religion as general foundations for belief in a future righteous order.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Sunni as well as Shi'ah narrations
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari emphasizes that reports concerning the Promised al-Mahdi are not confined to Shi'ah collections; he cites the existence of substantial Sunni-source material as part of his historical argument.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — The historical effect is the main question
concepts.explanation: Rather than simply cataloguing Qur'anic verses and hadith, Mutahhari says his principal concern is how belief in the Promised al-Mahdi affected Islamic history.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Imam 'Ali and the earth never being empty of God's proof
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari quotes the report of Imam 'Ali's conversation with Kumayl, emphasizing the principle that the earth is never empty of God's proof, whether that proof is manifest or hidden.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Mukhtar and the Mahdi claim
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari identifies Mukhtar's movement as an early historical example in which the Mahdi concept was used politically. Mukhtar presented Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah as the Promised Mahdi and himself as his representative.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — The Kaysanite development
concepts.explanation: After Muhammad ibn Hanafiyyah's death, followers associated with this movement maintained that he had not died and was hidden at Mount Radwa. Mutahhari presents this as part of the historical development of Mahdist ideas.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Zuhri's statement about the Ahl al-Bayt
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari cites Zuhri's reaction to Zayd ibn 'Ali's uprising as evidence that expectation of a future successful rising from the Prophet's family was already a recognizable idea in early Islamic discourse.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Nafs al-Zakiyyah and Mahdism
concepts.explanation: The chapter discusses Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah, known as Nafs al-Zakiyyah, and the way people connected claims about him with Mahdism because of lineage, name and other reported signs.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Imam al-Sadiq rejects a false Mahdi claim
concepts.explanation: When invited to support Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah's uprising, Imam al-Sadiq distinguished between supporting an uprising for enjoining good and forbidding evil and accepting the claim that Muhammad was the Promised Mahdi. He rejected the latter identification.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Why Mahdist claims repeatedly appeared
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that the recurrence of Mahdist claims around various Alawi figures itself indicates how deeply established expectation of a future Mahdi was in the Muslim community.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — The Abbasid use of the name al-Mahdi
concepts.explanation: The chapter notes that an Abbasid caliph was also named al-Mahdi, illustrating how the Mahdi concept had political and historical resonance beyond one specific doctrinal community.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Distinguishing historical claims from proof
concepts.explanation: A recurring exam point is that the existence of historical claims about a person being Mahdi does not itself prove the claim. Mutahhari distinguishes what people claimed from what he presents as the underlying doctrinal/historical evidence.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Mansur's political use of the Mahdi name
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari reports that Mansur named his son Mahdi and, according to the historical accounts he cites, sometimes used the name politically while privately acknowledging that neither his son nor 'Abd Allah al-Mahdi was the promised figure.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Muhammad ibn 'Ijlan's allegiance
concepts.explanation: The case of the Medinan scholar Muhammad ibn 'Ijlan illustrates the danger of confusing a claimant with the promised Mahdi. He pledged allegiance to 'Abd Allah al-Mahdi because he believed him to be the promised figure; scholars intervened on his behalf.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Early Muslim disputes were about identity, not existence
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that early disagreements generally concerned which individual was the Mahdi, rather than whether the promised Mahdi existed at all. He cites disputes concerning Imam al-Kazim, Imam al-Baqir, Imam al-Sadiq and others.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Imam al-Sadiq and Isma'il's death
concepts.explanation: The chapter recounts how Imam al-Sadiq publicly demonstrated that his son Isma'il had died, specifically to prevent people from later claiming that Isma'il was the hidden Mahdi.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Di'bil's lamentation and Imam al-Rida
concepts.explanation: Di'bil recited a lamentation before Imam al-Rida naming tragedies suffered by the Ahl al-Bayt. Imam al-Rida added a reference to a grave in Tus, identifying it as his own future grave, and the poem also connected the history of suffering with the eventual reappearance of an Imam.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Mahdism as a Sunni historical phenomenon
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari argues that Mahdism cannot be treated as exclusively Shi'ah by pointing to Sunni populations and historical figures who accepted or claimed Mahdist ideas.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — False Mahdis
concepts.explanation: The existence of false claimants is presented as another historical consequence of widespread belief in the promised Mahdi. Mutahhari distinguishes the existence of impostors from the truth of the underlying belief.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Historical references in Hafiz's poetry
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari notes Mahdist imagery in poems attributed to Hafiz, while explicitly saying he cannot establish whether Hafiz was Shi'ah or Sunni. The point is the presence of Mahdist expectation in Persian literary culture.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Reform is not the enemy of reappearance
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari addresses a dangerous interpretation: some people might think society must become maximally corrupt before the Imam can reappear, and therefore reform should be opposed. He rejects this reasoning.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — The 'abscess' analogy
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari uses an abscess analogy to explain a revolutionary model in which accumulated corruption must reach a breaking point. He then contrasts this with the Islamic obligation to pursue reform rather than deliberately increase corruption.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Reappearance does not suspend religious duties
concepts.explanation: Waiting for Imam al-Mahdi does not cancel prayer, fasting, zakat, Hajj, enjoining good, forbidding evil, or other personal and social obligations. Mutahhari presents this as a direct rejection of passive or destructive interpretations of waiting.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Awaiting the Imam requires action
concepts.explanation: The correct expectation of reappearance is compatible with fulfilling religious duties and training individuals and society. The believer does not create corruption in order to accelerate the promised transformation.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — The end of the historical discussion
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari closes the historical survey by moving from evidence for widespread Mahdist belief to the philosophical and practical meaning of awaiting the reappearance.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Justice after tyranny is not a command to produce tyranny
concepts.explanation: The promise that justice will follow oppression does not mean believers should permit or create oppression. The promised future is not a justification for abandoning present moral responsibility.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — The core practical implication
concepts.explanation: The chapter connects Mahdism to active religious responsibility: personal worship, social obligations and moral reform remain valid while awaiting the Imam.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Core evidence chain
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari's historical chain is: Qur'anic promises → Prophetic reports → Imam 'Ali's statements → early Islamic Mahdist movements and claims → Sunni and Shi'ah historical evidence → practical meaning of awaiting reappearance.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Distinguish belief from political appropriation
concepts.explanation: A major exam distinction is between the doctrinal belief in a promised Mahdi and historical actors who appropriated the concept to legitimize political movements or particular claimants.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Distinguish evidence from interpretation
concepts.explanation: Mutahhari repeatedly separates historical reports from his interpretation of their significance. Statements such as why a claimant acted, whether someone privately believed a claim, or how a movement should be judged may remain matters of interpretation.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Overall conclusion of Chapter 8
concepts.explanation: The two-part chapter connects universal justice with Mahdism: justice is presented as the long-term direction of prophetic history, while the promised reappearance represents the culmination of that trajectory in a transformed human society.

concepts.title: Ch8 P2 — Awaiting as faith and responsibility
concepts.explanation: The closing emphasis is that genuine awaiting is not passive pessimism. Mutahhari describes awaiting the reappearance as an expression of faith that coexists with worship, moral discipline, social responsibility and hope for humanity.
